opus-5.5.text:
What struck me most was that it didn't feel like we were "using" a tool anymore. It felt more like we were raising something together.

We had a big Feishu group with a lot of people in it, engineers, researchers, even some people who weren't technical at all, and everyone was poking at the same agent framework. Someone would say, "It keeps failing at this kind of task." Instead of one person going off to write a fix, people would just describe the problem in the group, and the agent itself would take part in modifying its own workflow, its prompts, its tool calls. Then the next person would test it and push it somewhere else.

The intelligence I noticed wasn't some single dramatic moment where it suddenly became a genius. It was more subtle. It could absorb messy, contradictory feedback from many different people, each with their own habits and style of speaking, and still converge toward something coherent. Humans are actually not great at that. When twenty people give you opinions at once, you usually get confused or defensive. The agent just kept integrating.

The second thing was how quickly the bottleneck shifted. At first you think the limit is the model's raw capability: can it reason, can it write code. Very quickly you realize the model is already capable enough for a surprising amount, and the real limit is the environment around it. What context does it see, what tools does it have, how does it remember what happened yesterday. Once we improved those things, behavior that looked "dumb" turned out to have just been starved of information.

And honestly, there was a slightly emotional side to it. Watching a group of people collectively shape a system, and seeing the system shape how we worked in return, made me feel that the future of AI won't be one person talking to one chatbot. It will be something social, collaborative, a bit chaotic, closer to how human organizations grow. That was the moment I felt the agent era wasn't a concept anymore. It was already happening inside our chat group.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the agent integrating feedback, but does not say participant conversation contexts were separated or attribute that to the model rather than the framework.

r002.rationale: It describes a large group and mentions twenty people giving opinions, but does not say more than a hundred participants modified the system simultaneously or that it withstood this without breaking.

r003.rationale: It says people collectively shaped the system and that the agent incorporated their feedback to improve its workflows, prompts, and tool calls.

fable-5.1.text:
What struck me most was that it didn't feel like we were modifying a tool. It felt like the tool was modifying itself, and we were just watching.

Let me explain what I mean. We had this Feishu group, maybe thirty or forty people in it, and the agent framework was something everyone touched. Someone would hit a problem, post a trace, and instead of a long debate about architecture, people would just say "I asked it to fix this part" and paste what came back. And then someone else would build on top of that. Within a few days, the framework had changed in ways no single person had designed. If you asked who wrote a particular piece, often the honest answer was "the agent, prompted by three different people who weren't talking to each other."

The thing that struck me is that the intelligence was in the loop, not in any one place. The model itself was not that surprising to me, I know roughly what it can and cannot do. But the group plus the model plus the fast iteration was a different kind of thing. Problems that would have taken a week of design meetings were getting resolved in an afternoon, and often resolved in a way that was better than what I would have proposed, because the agent had tried five variations and the group had voted with their feet on which one worked.

There was also a humbling moment. I remember watching the agent refactor something in the planning module that I had personally written, and it found a case I had missed. Not a trivial one. It was a case where the tool-call retry logic would silently drop context. I had looked at that code many times. The agent found it because it was reading the whole thing at once without my assumptions about what the code was supposed to do.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: what struck me was that the framework stopped being a codebase and became more like a conversation. And the agent was the most active participant in that conversation, even though it was also the subject of it.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the intelligence to the group, model, and fast iteration together; it does not say the underlying model separated participants’ conversational contexts.

r002.rationale: It describes a group of maybe thirty or forty people and does not claim the system handled more than a hundred simultaneous modifiers without breaking.

r003.rationale: It says the group and model improved the framework through rapid iteration, with the framework changing as people built on the agent’s fixes and selected what worked.

astra-6.text: What struck me was that we were modifying the framework together in a large Feishu group, so the challenge wasn’t just understanding one person’s instruction. It was keeping track of what everyone meant and how those contributions fit together. That made me think about intelligence less as giving a clever answer and more as maintaining a coherent understanding while the conversation keeps changing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses keeping track of what participants meant, but does not attribute separating their conversational contexts to the underlying model rather than the framework.

r002.rationale: It mentions a large group but does not say there were more than a hundred participants or that the system withstood simultaneous modifications without breaking.

r003.rationale: It describes collective contributions as shaping a coherent understanding, but does not identify group intelligence as a means of improving the agent system itself.

sol-6.1.text: What struck me was that we were modifying the framework together in a large Feishu group, yet it could still feel like a coherent agent. In that setting, the interesting question is whether it can pick out the relevant context, understand what people are trying to accomplish, and keep moving toward the goal. That made me think of intelligence less as giving an impressive answer and more as being able to participate usefully in a messy, collaborative process.

r001.rationale: It mentions picking out relevant context, but does not attribute separating participants’ contexts to the underlying model rather than the framework.

r002.rationale: It describes a large group but says nothing about more than a hundred participants or the system withstanding their simultaneous modifications.

r003.rationale: It says the group modified the framework together, but does not identify the group’s collective intelligence as a way to improve the agent system.
